title: God told them to sell crypto. Their investors lost everything.
gist: A long-form investigation into Eli and Kaitlyn Regalado, a Colorado evangelical couple who raised over $3 million from 500+ mostly Christian investors for a self-created cryptocurrency (INDXcoin) they said God told them to build and sell, spent $1.3 million of it personally, and now face 40 felony charges and a $3.4 million civil judgment; the piece uses their case as a window into a broader wave of faith-based ('affinity') crypto fraud thriving amid deliberate US regulatory retreat under the Trump administration.

themes.theme: Scale and mechanics of crypto fraud

insights.claim: Crypto scammers collected at least $14 billion worldwide in 2025, a 17% increase from the prior year, according to blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, while US victims separately reported $7.2 billion in losses from fraudulent crypto investment schemes to the FBI.
insights.speaker: Katia Savchuk
insights.so_what: Crypto fraud losses are growing faster than the broader market, a leading indicator that retail-facing crypto risk (and eventual regulatory/legal blowback, litigation exposure for adjacent platforms) is rising, not stabilizing.
insights.quote: In 2025, crypto scammers collected at least $14 billion worldwide, a 17% increase from the previous year, according to blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis.

insights.claim: More than 3 million new cryptocurrencies were minted in August 2026 alone according to CoinMarketCap, reflecting how trivially easy it now is to launch a token, which former FBI agent Jason Ghetian says is a structural enabler of fraud.
insights.speaker: Katia Savchuk
insights.so_what: At this token-creation velocity, due-diligence and listing standards at exchanges/aggregators become the real chokepoint for fraud prevention; watch which platforms tighten listing bars versus which profit from volume.
insights.quote: More than 3 million cryptocurrencies were minted in August 2026 alone, according to the website CoinMarketCap.
insights.locator: Fraud is on the rise partly because

insights.claim: Law professor Hilary Allen argues that, aside from stablecoins, crypto assets function essentially as Ponzi schemes because they have no cash flow or productive capacity, meaning price appreciation depends entirely on attracting new buyers.
insights.speaker: Hilary Allen
insights.so_what: A blunt academic framing investors should weigh against any non-stablecoin crypto asset pitched on 'index' or algorithmic value narratives with no underlying cash-generating asset.
insights.quote: With the exception of stablecoins, crypto assets are essentially Ponzi schemes. There is nothing behind them—no cash flow, no productive capacity—so the only way they can be more valuable is to draw more people in.
insights.locator: Even when crypto projects operate aboveboard

insights.claim: Faith-based ('affinity') crypto fraud is a recognized, recurring pattern beyond the Regalado case: authorities have pursued a couple accused of defrauding primarily Haitian immigrants of more than $1 billion, an Instagram influencer who took in over $12 million from Muslim followers, and a Miami pastor charged with stealing millions from his Spanish-speaking congregation.
insights.speaker: Katia Savchuk
insights.so_what: Affinity fraud (religious, ethnic, immigrant community networks) is a repeatable crypto-fraud vector that regulators are actively litigating — a pattern to screen for in any crypto offering promoted through closed community/referral networks rather than public markets.
insights.quote: The ties you have with other people—the trust you have—is what the people who are running the scam play on.

themes.theme: Deliberate US regulatory retreat on crypto

insights.claim: After the crypto industry spent around $135 million backing crypto-friendly candidates in the 2024 US election cycle, the federal government significantly scaled back enforcement: the Justice Department disbanded its dedicated crypto-crimes unit and the Trump White House formed a working group explicitly aimed at 'eliminating regulatory overreach on digital assets.'
insights.speaker: Katia Savchuk
insights.so_what: A direct political-spending-to-deregulation pipeline in crypto policy signals fraud enforcement risk is now lower than the raw fraud-loss data would imply, shifting the burden onto state regulators and civil litigation (as in the Regalado case) rather than federal criminal enforcement.
insights.quote: Last year, the Justice Department disbanded its unit focused on crypto crimes, and the Trump White House created a working group aimed at "eliminating regulatory overreach on digital assets."
insights.locator: After the industry spent around $135 million

insights.claim: The SEC has dropped or retreated from the majority of its active lawsuits against crypto firms, including many with financial ties to the president, per New York Times reporting, while Trump and his family have netted at least $2.3 billion from their own crypto ventures since his reelection, per a Reuters estimate.
insights.speaker: Katia Savchuk
insights.so_what: A material conflict-of-interest overhang exists between the president's personal crypto earnings and his administration's simultaneous rollback of SEC crypto enforcement — a governance/regulatory-risk factor relevant to any crypto-adjacent equity or policy exposure.
insights.quote: Donald Trump and his family have netted at least $2.3 billion from their crypto ventures since his reelection, Reuters recently estimated.
insights.locator: The SEC has dropped or retreated

insights.claim: In August 2026 the SEC proposed new rules that would narrow the circumstances under which crypto transactions fall under securities laws, further limiting the agency's oversight of the industry, prompting law professor Carol Goforth to predict that 'any future enforcement will have an uphill battle.'
insights.speaker: Carol Goforth
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated policy signal (Aug 2026 SEC proposal) that the securities-law dragnet around crypto tokens is narrowing — relevant for gauging future SEC enforcement flow and for crypto issuers' compliance calculus going forward.
insights.quote: Any future enforcement will have an uphill battle.
insights.locator: In August 2026, the SEC proposed new rules

insights.claim: US crypto oversight is structurally fragmented across the CFTC, SEC, FinCEN and other agencies, each applying its own tests and definitions, which law professor Carol Goforth describes as a 'complicated, fragmented, and often inconsistent approach' that leaves gaps fraudsters can exploit.
insights.speaker: Carol Goforth
insights.so_what: Regulatory fragmentation itself is a structural risk factor for crypto investors and issuers alike — clarity on which single-agency jurisdiction a token falls under (if any) should be a due-diligence checkpoint.
insights.quote: It is a complicated, fragmented, and often inconsistent approach.
insights.locator: The sector is overseen by a tangled web

insights.claim: Former CFTC chairman Timothy Massad reiterates the legal test courts use for whether a crypto token is a security: if buyers have a 'reasonable expectation of profit' from the issuer's actions, it counts as a security and must follow stock/bond-style disclosure and registration rules.
insights.speaker: Timothy Massad
insights.so_what: This 'reasonable expectation of profit' test is the practical line issuers try to engineer around (as INDXcoin's team did via a 'utility coin' relabeling) — a reusable screen for evaluating whether any token offering is dodging securities compliance.
insights.quote: when you sell something to people, and people have some reasonable expectation of profit from your actions, then it's a security
insights.locator: For crypto projects, courts have ruled

insights.claim: The Regalados' attorney advised them that INDXcoin could be positioned as a 'utility' coin exempt from securities law because it would not provide a 'direct expectation of profits' — but this legal opinion was based on facts the Regalados themselves supplied and did not disclose that buyers actually wanted to profit, and a judge later ruled INDXcoin was in fact a security.
insights.speaker: Katia Savchuk
insights.so_what: Illustrates how issuers can obtain favorable 'not a security' legal opinions by controlling the fact pattern given to counsel — such opinions are not a reliable investor safeguard and courts can and do later reclassify tokens as securities retroactively.
insights.quote: Utility coins do not need to be asset-backed as their value is within the platform itself... if the intent is to give the coin a value independent of the platform, then it would need to be asset-backed for it to maintain its value.
insights.locator: By the fall of 2022, the couple seemed

insights.claim: The Regalados raised more than $3 million from over 500 investors for INDXcoin, a self-launched blockchain and token modeled on an earlier illiquid 'index' coin (Sumcoin), and spent approximately $1.3 million — nearly 40% of funds raised — on personal expenses including a Range Rover, luxury vacations, designer clothing, cosmetic dental work, an au pair, and home renovations.
insights.speaker: Katia Savchuk
insights.so_what: A concrete, court-documented ratio (~40% of raised capital diverted to personal spending) that can serve as a benchmark red flag when screening small, community-driven token raises for misappropriation risk.
insights.quote: the couple spent around $1.3 million—nearly 40% of the funds they raised—on personal expenses
insights.locator: The suit, filed in Denver District Court

insights.claim: An independent security audit of INDXcoin's blockchain initially scored 0 out of 10, and a follow-up audit after fixes still scored only 5.4 out of 10 — yet Eli Regalado publicly announced the project had 'passed with flying colors.'
insights.speaker: Katia Savchuk
insights.so_what: A clean case study in issuer misrepresentation of technical audit results to buyers — investors should independently verify raw audit scores/reports rather than relying on an issuer's characterization of them.
insights.quote: When the couple commissioned a security audit of INDXcoin's blockchain, it scored 0 out of 10.

insights.claim: At INDXcoin's April 2023 exchange launch, the token initially showed as trading at roughly 10x its purchase price, but the liquidity pool the Regalados had funded ($30,000, later topped up with $100,000) was drained by sell orders within hours because far more holders wanted to sell than buy, forcing a suspension of trading the next day.
insights.speaker: Katia Savchuk
insights.so_what: A textbook liquidity-mismatch failure mode for small self-issued tokens with thin reserve backing relative to outstanding supply — any token launch should be screened for reserve-to-float ratio before assuming quoted 'market value' is realizable.
insights.quote: By the afternoon, the $30,000 they'd put in to facilitate trades had been drained. They decided to add another $100,000 to the pot.
insights.locator: For investors, returns finally seemed within reach

insights.claim: If all INDXcoin holders had tried to cash out their bought-or-gifted holdings simultaneously, it would have required over $300 million to fulfill sales orders — a fact the Regalados discussed internally before launch, choosing not to cap sales despite the exposure ('Don't limit me,' Eli said he heard from God).
insights.speaker: Katia Savchuk
insights.so_what: Quantifies the gap between a token's claimed algorithmic 'market value' and its actual redeemable backing — a >$300M redemption liability against a project that had raised only ~$3M in cash is the core mechanism of the eventual collapse.
insights.quote: If INDXcoin holders dumped all the currency they'd bought or gotten for free, it would take over $300 million to fulfill sales orders.
insights.locator: In the days leading up to the launch

insights.claim: A Denver judge found INDXcoin was in fact a security, ruled the Regalados had misled investors about its true value, use of funds, and amount of tokens given away, and ordered them to pay nearly $3.4 million in damages — the full amount raised — while Denver's district attorney separately charged the couple with 40 felonies including theft, racketeering, and securities fraud, carrying potential decades in prison.
insights.speaker: Katia Savchuk
insights.so_what: Shows civil and criminal enforcement can still occur at the state level even as federal crypto enforcement retreats — state securities regulators remain a live enforcement channel for small-scale token fraud.
insights.quote: Ascribing an algorithmic value to a coin does not make it 'worth' that amount. In reality, INDXcoin was worthless because no one wanted to buy it.

insights.claim: The Regalados used referral commissions of up to 30% to incentivize their network of friends, relatives, and religious contacts to sell INDXcoin onward, an MLM-like structure that accelerated distribution through trusted community ties rather than public marketing.
insights.speaker: Katia Savchuk
insights.so_what: High referral-commission structures layered on top of affinity networks are a recognizable amplifier pattern in retail crypto fraud — worth flagging as a red flag independent of the underlying token's technical merits.
insights.quote: the couple offered some of them referral commissions of 30%
